bib.title: Google’s Neural Machine Translation System: Bridging the Gap between Human and Machine Translation

read.skipped: Reference list skimmed; Table 11 examples and Figure 6 histogram not read in detail.

question: Can a deep LSTM NMT system be made fast, robust to rare words and accurate enough to replace a phrase-based production translation system?
hypothesis: Residual deep LSTMs with attention, wordpiece units, quantized inference and a coverage-penalised beam search close the gap with PBMT and approach human translation.
contributions: GNMT: 8-layer encoder/decoder LSTM with residual connections and bottom-to-top attention
Wordpiece model (8K-32K shared vocab) for open vocabulary
Model and data parallelism for training in about a week
Length normalization and coverage penalty in beam search
RL refinement with GLEU reward (no human gain)

method.summary: Seq2seq LSTM with 8 encoder (1 bidirectional) and 8 decoder layers, residual connections, feed-forward attention from bottom decoder layer to top encoder layer, wordpiece segmentation, ML training then optional RL refinement, quantization-aware training and beam search with length/coverage score.
method.task: neural machine translation (WMT'14 En->Fr, En->De, Google production pairs)

datasets.name: WMT'14 En->Fr
datasets.preprocessing: Shared source/target wordpiece model 8K/16K/32K; tokenized BLEU

datasets.name: Google production data (En<->Fr, En<->Es, En<->Zh)
datasets.size: two to three decimal orders of magnitude bigger than WMT
datasets.split: 500 randomly sampled Wikipedia and news sentences per pair for human evaluation

models.name: GNMT (WPM-32K)
models.architecture: 8-layer encoder (bottom bidirectional) + 8-layer decoder LSTM, residual connections from third layer, attention
models.hidden: 1024 LSTM nodes per layer; attention FFN one hidden layer with 1024 nodes

other.char model: a few hundred basic characters (En->De char model 512 nodes)

models.name: PBMT
models.architecture: phrase-based MT (Durrani et al. WMT14 for En->Fr; Buck et al. for En->De; Google production)

training.objective: ML sum log P(Y*|X) (eq 7); optional refinement with alpha*O_ML + O_RL, alpha typically 0.017, GLEU reward, mean-reward baseline from m=15 samples
training.optimizer: Adam for first 60k steps then plain SGD (async, Downpour-style, 12 replicas)
training.lr_schedule: En->Fr: anneal after 1.2M steps, halve every 200k steps for an additional 800k steps
training.steps: ML: about 2M (inferred from 1.2M + 800k annealing); RL refinement 400k steps on En->Fr
training.precision: full-precision float in training, with clipping constraints for quantization
training.dropout: 0.2 En->Fr, 0.3 En->De; ML phase only; none on production data
training.regularisation: gradient clipping norm 5.0; uniform init [-0.04, 0.04]; accumulator clipping
training.hardware: 96 NVIDIA K80 GPUs for En->Fr basic model; each replica partitioned 8-way over GPUs
training.compute: about 6 days ML + about 3 days RL (En->Fr)
training.wall_clock: about 6 days ML; about 3 days RL
training.seeds: 8 models trained per configuration; test numbers use model chosen on dev

inference.decoding: beam search with length normalization and coverage penalty; typically 8-12 hypotheses kept, beamsize 3.0 pruning; batch up to 35 similar-length sentences
inference.samples: test BLEU averaged over 8 models; single decode per model

parameters.table 4 timing: CPU, batch 16 sentences, max 4 concurrent hypotheses

other.quantization: 8-bit weights, 16-bit accumulators and elementwise ops; attention and softmax not quantized

metrics.name: Side-by-side human score
metrics.definition: raters fluent in both languages score translations 0 (nonsense) to 6 (perfect)

metrics.name: CPU decoding time per sentence
metrics.definition: total decoding time / number of sentences

baselines: PBMT (Edinburgh WMT14, Buck et al., Google production)
eval.protocol: Test numbers from model picked on dev; 8 models averaged; human SxS on 500 sentences; no significance test reported

evidence.quote:
we begin to anneal the
learning rate after 1.2M steps, after which we halve the learning rate every 200k steps for an additional 800k steps.

results.claim: GNMT WPM-32K single model reaches 38.95 BLEU on WMT En->Fr newstest2014, averaged over 8 trained models.
results.setup: WMT'14 En->Fr, 36M pairs, ML-trained, shared 32K wordpiece vocab, tokenized BLEU via multi-bleu.pl; mean of 8 models
results.quote:
Our best model, WPM-32K, achieves a BLEU score of 38.95. Note that this BLEU score represents the
averaged score of 8 models we trained.

results.claim: Best of the 8 WPM-32K models scores 39.37 BLEU on En->Fr.
results.setup: same as above; maximum of 8 models
results.quote: The maximum BLEU score of the 8 models is higher at 39.37.

results.claim: Word model vs character model vs wordpiece on En->Fr: word 37.90, character 38.01, WPM-32K 38.95.
results.setup: WMT En->Fr newstest2014, single ML models; word model 212K source/80K target vocab with attention copy of UNKs
results.table: Table 4, rows Word / Character / WPM-32K, column BLEU (37.90, 38.01, 38.95)

results.claim: Other En->Fr vocabularies: WPM-8K 38.27, WPM-16K 37.60, mixed word/character (32K) 38.39; WPM-16K is below the word model.
results.setup: WMT En->Fr newstest2014, single ML models
results.table: Table 4, rows WPM-8K, WPM-16K, Mixed Word/Character, column BLEU (38.27, 37.60, 38.39)

results.claim: Character model decodes about 5x slower than WPM-32K on CPU (1.0530 s vs 0.2118 s per sentence).
results.setup: CPU decoding, batch 16 sentences, max 4 concurrent hypotheses, WMT En->Fr newstest2014; time per sentence = total decode time / sentences
results.table: Table 4, rows Character and WPM-32K, column CPU decoding time per sentence (s): 1.0530 vs 0.2118

results.claim: WPM-32K gets 24.61 BLEU on WMT En->De, averaged over 8 runs, vs 23.12 for word model.
results.note: Table 6 prints the ML-trained En->De single-model average as 24.67, Table 5 prints WPM-32K as 24.61.
results.quote: Our best model, WPM-32K, achieves a BLEU score of 24.61, which is averaged over 8 runs.

results.claim: Wordpiece/mixed models give more than 2 BLEU over the word model on En->De.
results.quote:
which provide a gain of more than 2 BLEU points on top of the word model and about 4 BLEU points on top of previously reported
results in [6, 45]

results.claim: RL refinement improves En->Fr single-model BLEU from 38.95 to 39.92 but slightly lowers En->De (24.67 to 24.60).
results.setup: avg of 8 independent models, test BLEU, dropout off in RL phase
results.table: Table 6, row En->Fr, columns Trained with log-likelihood / Refined with RL: 38.95, 39.92

results.claim: Ensemble of 8 RL-refined WPM-32K models gets 41.16 BLEU on En->Fr; ML-only ensemble 40.35.
results.quote:
We ensemble 8 RL-reﬁned models to obtain a state-of-the-art result of 41.16 BLEU points on the WMT
En→Fr dataset.

results.claim: Ensemble of 8 RL-refined models gets 26.30 BLEU on En->De.
results.quote:
We ensemble 8 RL-reﬁned models to obtain a state-of-the-art result of 26.30 BLEU points on the WMT
En→De dataset.

results.claim: RL gain in BLEU did not show in human evaluation: SxS 4.46 before RL vs 4.44 after (PBMT 3.87, human 4.82).
results.table: Table 9, rows NMT before RL / NMT after RL, column Side-by-side averaged score: 4.46, 4.44

results.claim: GNMT reduces translation errors by more than 60% vs PBMT on production data for En<->Fr/Es/Zh.
results.setup: 500 random sentences per pair from Wikipedia and news, human SxS 0-6, single wordpiece 32K models, no ensemble, no RL
results.note: Table 10 relative improvements per pair: 87%, 64%, 58%, 63%, 83%, 60%; the En->Zh value 58% is below 60%.
results.quote:
results show that our model reduces translation errors by more than 60% compared to the PBMT model on
these major pairs of languages.

results.claim: Abstract states 60% average error reduction on isolated simple sentences.
results.setup: human SxS vs Google PBMT production
results.quote:
it reduces translation errors by an average of
60% compared to Google’s phrase-based production system.

results.claim: TPU quantized decoding is 3.4x faster than CPU with no BLEU loss (31.21 vs 31.20) and log perplexity 1.4626 vs 1.4553.
results.setup: WMT En->Fr dev set (newstest2012+2013, 6003 sentences), ML+quantization-constrained model; CPU/GPU full precision; 88-core host; K80 GPU; one TPU
results.table: Table 1, rows CPU/GPU/TPU, columns BLEU, Log Perplexity, Decoding time (s): 31.20/1.4553/1322; 31.20/1.4553/3028; 31.21/1.4626/384

results.claim: CPU decoding is 2.3x faster than GPU in their implementation.
results.quote: Table 1 also shows that decoding our model on CPU is actually 2.3 times faster than on GPU.

results.claim: Length normalization and coverage penalty raise dev BLEU from 30.3 to 31.4 (alpha=0.2, beta=0.2: +1.1).
results.setup: WMT En->Fr dev set, ML-only model, beam search
results.quote:
having some length normalization and coverage penalty
improves BLEU score considerably (from 30.3 to 31.4)

results.claim: Training WMT En->Fr takes about 6 days on 96 K80 GPUs; RL refinement 3 days for 400k steps.
results.quote: it takes around 6 days to train a basic model using 96 NVIDIA K80 GPUs.

results.claim: Plain stacked LSTMs work up to 4 layers, barely at 6, very poorly beyond 8.
results.setup: large-scale translation tasks, no residual connections; anecdotal, no table
results.quote:
simple stacked LSTM layers work well up to 4 layers, barely
with 6 layers, and very poorly beyond 8 layers.

results.claim: Adam for first 60k steps then SGD converges better than Adam alone or SGD alone.
results.setup: WMT En->Fr ML training, log perplexity (read from Fig 5)
results.quote: We run Adam for the ﬁrst 60k steps, after which we switch to simple SGD.

limits: RL refinement raised BLEU but not human SxS scores; authors suspect small sample (500) and BLEU/quality mismatch.
Production human evaluation uses simple isolated sentences; difficult cases and longer inputs left as future work.
Human translations score only about 5 of 6, indicating noisy raters.
WMT En->De RL refinement slightly hurt test BLEU.
Hyperparameters vary by dataset and model and are not fully listed; code and weights not released; parameter count not stated.
Wordpiece algorithm details deferred to Schuster and Nakajima 2012.

terms.definition: Select D wordpieces such that the resulting corpus is minimal in the number of wordpieces when segmented according to the chosen wordpiece model; special symbol marks word beginning.
minimum of n-gram recall and precision (1-4 grams) between output and target
